title: Most Back-to-Back Copies of a Word
statement:
You get two strings, text and word. Writing word c times in a row with nothing between the copies gives the string word × c; for example "ab" × 3 = "ababab".

Return the largest c such that word × c appears in text as a contiguous substring. If word does not appear at all, return 0. Copies scattered across text with other letters between them do not add up.

examples.why: "xyxy" appears at the start. "xyxyxy" does not appear anywhere.
"aaaa" appears after the b, but "aaaaaa" does not. Counting non-overlapping copies over the whole text would wrongly give 3.
"abaaba" starts at index 2, in the middle of the first copy at index 0. A scan that jumps past the first copy and restarts after it misses this run.

constraints: Both strings use lowercase English letters
hints: Simplest version: try c = 1, 2, 3, … and check whether word repeated c times is inside text. When can you stop?
To avoid rebuilding strings, think about where a run of copies ends. If a copy of word ends at position i, what can you say about the run ending at i − word.length?
Let run[i] be the number of back-to-back copies ending exactly at position i. If text[i − m .. i) equals word, then run[i] = run[i − m] + 1, otherwise 0. The answer is the largest run[i].

explain.intuition:
The direct approach works well at this size: keep making the repeated word longer and test whether text contains it. If word × c is missing, every longer repetition is missing too, because it contains word × c. So you stop at the first failure.

A neater idea looks at where runs end. Let run[i] count how many copies sit back to back and end exactly at position i (exclusive). If the m characters before i spell word, this copy extends whatever run ended just before it: run[i] = run[i − m] + 1. Otherwise run[i] = 0. Every start position is considered, so overlapping candidates like the one in "ababaaba" are never skipped.
steps: Let n = text.length, m = word.length, and run an array of n + 1 zeros.
For i from m to n: if text.slice(i − m, i) === word, set run[i] = run[i − m] + 1.
Return it (0 if no copy matched).
pitfalls: Jumping forward by m after a failed run and restarting from there. The best run may start inside the copy you skipped over.
Counting all copies of word in the text instead of copies that touch each other.
Stopping the repeat test early because word × c is longer than text but forgetting to return the previous c, not c itself.

solutions.title: Grow the repetition until it no longer fits
solutions.idea: Test word, word × 2, word × 3, … against text. The first missing one ends the search.

solutions.title: Runs that end at each position
solutions.idea: run[i] = run[i − m] + 1 when a copy of word ends at i. The answer is the largest run.

followups: Text has 10⁶ characters. How would KMP or a rolling hash make each copy test O(1)?
Return where the longest run starts, choosing the leftmost one on ties.
